summary:
Mauritius decriminalised same-sex conduct on 4 October 2023, when the Supreme Court struck down Section 250 of the Criminal Code of 1838 as unconstitutional, ruling that it must be read to exclude consensual acts. The provision had carried penal servitude of up to five years. Prosecutions were rare: the US State Department's 2016 country report found that sodomy references arose overwhelmingly in heterosexual divorce proceedings as an aggravating factor, although a same-sex couple was arrested in 2015 on suspicion of practising sodomy. In October 2019 a group of young people filed a constitutional challenge to Section 250, supported by the Young Queer Alliance and the Love Honor Cherish Foundation, alongside activist Abdool Ridwan Firaas Ah Seek, 29, backed by Collectif Arc-En-Ciel.

Legal gender recognition is not available in Mauritius. The Civil Status Act of 1981 and the Central Population Database form the framework under which trans people are not recognised, and Outright International's country overview, last updated 12 March 2026, states that legal gender recognition is not possible. An AfricLaw analysis of 23 August 2024, written by Lakshita Kanhiya, concludes that legal recognition and protection for trans Mauritians remain inadequate. The Young Queer Alliance's July 2021 policy brief on administrative recognition of trans people argues for legal gender recognition and calls on Mauritius to join the countries recognising gender identity in law, noting that the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders in 2019.

Outright International's overview records that advances since decriminalisation have been noted for lesbian, gay and bisexual people, with progress for trans or intersex people 'less evident'. No same-sex marriage or civil union is recognised. The Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation; no equivalent protection covering gender identity is stated in the sources. Intersex newborns may be registered as 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act, but nonconsensual intersex medical procedures are not banned. LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Discrimination and harassment are documented. The US State Department's 2016 report records societal discrimination, with LGBTI victims of family verbal abuse or violence reporting to local NGOs including Collectif Arc-en-Ciel and the Young Queer Alliance, and documents the harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing. Outright International's 2026 overview notes that during the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and others used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech. LGBTQ people may face discrimination notably in public hospitals, according to the sources; the same sources state that hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals according to the government, while gender-affirming care is available only in limited form.

Public visibility carries a documented backlash history. Collectif Arc-En-Ciel, founded in 2005, organised the country's first Pride and has done so for fifteen years, drawing more than 1,200 participants in 2016 when the march moved from Rose-Hill to Port Louis. In 2018 the Pride march was annulled after hundreds of death threats believed to come from religious extremists, and a counter-protest was organised by Javed Meetoo, described as an Islamic extremist under state surveillance; a strong police force had been deployed earlier in 2018 to protect marchers, and an LGBTQ sit-in at the Caudan Waterfront followed with the Prime Minister's support. Outright International's 2026 overview states Pride has been held since 2005 with counter-protesters.

State and institutional actors have shown both support and hostility. Police protected Pride marchers, Prime Minister Pravind Jugnauth backed an LGBTQ sit-in, and the Opposition stated that sexual orientation should not be an obstacle to equal rights; Cardinal Maurice Piat and other religious leaders condemned the anti-LGBTQ protest and called for tolerance. Conservative attitudes remain commonplace and LGBTQ people still face discrimination, with bullying in schools documented, while acceptance is growing particularly among the younger generation; polls cited in the sources indicate Mauritius is one of Africa's most LGBTQ-friendly countries, and a 2016 poll found 49% of Mauritians would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour.

Documentation of day-to-day conditions: AfriGay reports that gay life is fairly quiet, existing mainly online, in private and at occasional parties, though resorts are welcoming and non-discriminatory and no problems with LGBTQ couples sharing hotel rooms have been recorded. In 2014 the Ministry of Health amended blood donation policy to allow men who have sex with men to donate, although the sources note that anecdotally LGBTQI persons have still been prevented from donating on occasion. The Young Queer Alliance was founded on 1 September 2014 for young LGBTQ Mauritians, engaging in support, advocacy and anti-discrimination campaigns; activism by the Young Queer Alliance and Association VISA-G is noted in the AfricLaw analysis. Visibility milestone: Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan was the first transgender woman to participate in Miss Universe Mauritius 2024.
tangentialFactors:
The 2023 decriminalisation judgment addressed only Section 250; it did not create gender-identity protections, partnership recognition or a gender-recognition procedure. Outright International's March 2026 overview separates the LGB advances from what it calls less evident progress for trans or intersex people, which is the clearest signal that a trans visitor should not read the 2023 ruling as covering trans-specific legal questions.

The 2024 election period produced anti-LGBTIQ hate speech from parliamentary candidates, including a characterisation of sexual and gender diversity as a 'Western deviation'. This is political rhetoric rather than enacted law, but it indicates the level of official hostility a gender-nonconforming visitor may encounter in public debate during an election period.

The 2018 cancellation of Pride after hundreds of death threats, and the counter-protest organised by a figure described as under state surveillance, is the most severe documented instance of organised anti-LGBTQ hostility in the record. Police protection of marchers and the Prime Minister's support for a subsequent sit-in cut the other way. The most recent documented instance of this class of organised threat in the record is 2018; no later instance is documented.

The sources rank or characterise Mauritius relative to other African jurisdictions on friendliness using polls, not on trans-specific measures. A 2016 poll found 49% of Mauritians would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour, and the sources describe Mauritius as one of Africa's most LGBTQ-friendly countries; neither figure measures trans-specific attitudes or violence.
